federal.heading: The federal picture
federal.intro: Most "federal grant" pages you'll find are out of date. Here's the verified state of the national programs:

items.name: National Heat Pump Rebate (new)
items.note: Announced October 8, 2026 and expected to open early 2027: $2,000 toward an eligible cold-climate air-source heat pump, or up to $10,000 for households below the median income. Apply online, approval within 24 hours, no EnerGuide evaluation, and it can be combined with provincial rebates. Not open yet.

items.name: Canada Greener Homes Grant & Loan
items.note: The grant closed to new applicants in February 2024; the interest-free loan (up to $40,000) stopped taking applications October 1, 2025 and its funding is fully committed. Approved applicants keep their funding — new ones can't join.

items.name: Greener Homes Affordability Program
items.note: Free direct-install retrofits (insulation, heat pumps) for low-to-median-income owners and tenants, expanded June 29, 2026 with over $500 million, delivered through provincial partners in BC, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, PEI and Quebec (Quebec's 2026–27 registration has ended), with more to be listed. You apply through your province's program, never through cold-callers.

noteByProvince.newfoundland-labrador: NRCan's list of delivery provinces doesn't include Newfoundland and Labrador yet, but takeCHARGE's income-eligible TakeCharge Greener Homes Program, "delivered in partnership with the Government of Canada", covers projects completed after October 5, 2026.

items.name: Oil to Heat Pump Affordability (OHPA)
items.note: Closed to new applications July 31, 2026 (approved participants have until January 31, 2027 to submit receipts). Where NRCan delivered it directly (Alberta, Manitoba, the Northwest Territories, Quebec and Saskatchewan), it paid up to $10,000 toward oil-to-heat-pump conversions for income-qualified households.

noteByProvince.bc: Closed to new applications July 31, 2026 (approved participants have until January 31, 2027 to submit receipts). It paid up to $15,000 (plus a one-time $250 payment) toward oil-to-heat-pump conversions for income-qualified households.
noteByProvince.new-brunswick: Closed to new applications July 31, 2026 (approved participants have until January 31, 2027 to submit receipts). It paid up to $15,000 (plus a one-time $250 payment) toward oil-to-heat-pump conversions for income-qualified households.
noteByProvince.newfoundland-labrador: Closed to new applications July 31, 2026 (approved participants have until January 31, 2027 to submit receipts). It paid up to $15,000 (plus a one-time $250 payment) toward oil-to-heat-pump conversions for income-qualified households. Newfoundland and Labrador's own Oil to Electric program is still accepting applications.
noteByProvince.pei: Closed to new applications July 31, 2026 (approved participants have until January 31, 2027 to submit receipts). It paid up to $15,000 (plus a one-time $250 payment) toward oil-to-heat-pump conversions for income-qualified households.
noteByProvince.nova-scotia: Closed to new applications July 31, 2026 (approved participants have until January 31, 2027 to submit receipts). It paid up to $15,000 (plus a one-time $250 payment) toward oil-to-heat-pump conversions for income-qualified households. Efficiency Nova Scotia stopped taking applications even earlier, on July 2, 2026.
noteByProvince.ontario: Closed to new applications July 31, 2026 (approved participants have until January 31, 2027 to submit receipts). It paid up to $15,000 (plus a one-time $250 payment) toward oil-to-heat-pump conversions for income-qualified households. In Ontario it was delivered with Save on Energy as a free heat pump installation worth up to $25,000.
noteByProvince.north: Closed to new applications July 31, 2026 (approved participants have until January 31, 2027 to submit receipts). In Yukon it paid up to $15,000 (plus a one-time $250 payment) toward oil-to-heat-pump conversions for income-qualified households, and in the Northwest Territories up to $10,000. Homes in Nunavut were not eligible.

provinces.name: British Columbia
provinces.intro: BC pairs ambitious building rules with an audit-linked rebate: the Home Energy Improvement Bonus pays by measured improvement between two EnerGuide evaluations. Add the Home Renovation Rebate program's per-upgrade rebates, income-tiered CleanBC rebates and free upgrades for lower-income households, and BC is one of the better places in the country to do a retrofit properly.
provinces.housing: Vancouver and the coast fight moisture more than cold — older stock leaks air and grows condensation problems in mild wet winters, and wildfire-smoke summers have made filtration a mainstream concern. The Interior and North are a different climate entirely: real winters, wood heat, and homes where envelope upgrades pay fast. Step Code-era new builds are tight and need their ventilation verified.

programs.name: Home Energy Improvement Bonus
programs.headline: $20 per %-point improvement · $750–$2,000
programs.note: Complete three bonus-eligible upgrades with pre- and post-upgrade EnerGuide evaluations within 18 months, apply within six months of the second evaluation, and get paid for the measured improvement. Doing only two upgrades? A separate $300 Two Upgrade Bonus needs no evaluation (one bonus per home). This is the audit-first model done right — the evaluations are the program.

programs.name: CleanBC Energy Savings Program
programs.headline: Income-tiered rebates · heat pumps to $13,000
programs.note: Lower- and middle-income households get rebates of up to 100% of eligible costs, capped by level (for example, up to $13,000 for a central heat pump replacing oil, gas or propane), paid through registered contractors. It isn't free installation, and its insulation rebates ended for invoices from July 6, 2026. Free upgrades come through BC Hydro's and FortisBC's programs, which also deliver the federal Affordability Program.

programs.name: Home Renovation Rebate (BC Hydro & FortisBC)
programs.headline: Heat pumps $4,000 · insulation · windows $100 each
programs.note: For any income: $4,000 for a whole-home heat pump replacing electric heat ($1,500 partial), insulation at $0.02–$0.09 × R-value added × sq ft, windows and doors $100 each up to $2,000 (not in the City of Vancouver) and $1,000 for an electric heat pump water heater. Rebates for switching from oil (up to $6,000) or gas and propane (up to $8,000) apply only north of and including 100 Mile House. BC Hydro adds up to $1,000 for an air-source heat pump completed and paid between August 1 and October 31, 2026, while funding lasts.

homeHealth.name: Smoke-season air
homeHealth.note: Wildfire smoke is now an annual season in much of BC. A PM2.5 monitor plus sized HEPA purifiers — with spare filters bought before summer — is the standing playbook.

homeHealth.name: Coastal moisture & mould
homeHealth.note: Mild, wet winters make ventilation the coast's defining home-health question. Diagnose ventilation vs. cold-surface before spending — the audit's assessment settles it.

homeHealth.name: Radon — Interior & North
homeHealth.note: Parts of the Interior test well above the coast in cross-Canada surveys, and every home tests individually. One 3-month winter kit answers it.

homeHealth.name: Rural wells
homeHealth.note: Testing regimes differ from Ontario's free-lab model — BC well owners typically test through private accredited labs; your health authority lists them. The routine (bacteria often, chemistry periodically) is the same.

provinces.name: Alberta
provinces.intro: Alberta has no provincial home energy rebate right now, which makes the audit's other jobs the story here: lower bills, right-sized equipment and pre-purchase clarity. Financing exists in the 27 municipalities that run a Clean Energy Improvement Program, which requires an EnerGuide evaluation, though Calgary's intake is closed until winter and Edmonton's is waitlisted.
provinces.housing: Calgary and Edmonton's stock skews newer than central Canada's, but the climate is unforgiving: design temperatures far below the national average make envelope quality the whole game. Older bungalow belts drill-and-fill beautifully; newer tight homes need ventilation verified. Chinook cycling in the south works building envelopes hard.

programs.name: Clean Energy Improvement Program (CEIP)
programs.headline: Property-tax financing, 27 municipalities
programs.note: Financing of up to 100% of upgrade costs, repaid on your property tax bill over up to 20 years for some upgrades, with an EnerGuide evaluation required. Calgary's residential intake is closed until winter 2026/27, Edmonton's pre-qualifications go on a waitlist (6.00%), and Lethbridge and Strathcona County are at capacity. Red Deer doesn't participate.

programs.name: Provincial rebates
programs.headline: None found
programs.note: We found no province-wide home energy rebate: the Government of Alberta's energy-efficiency programs page now returns "page not found", the City of Edmonton says it has no residential rebates, and the federal oil-to-heat-pump program, which NRCan ran directly here, closed July 31, 2026.

homeHealth.name: Radon — take it seriously here
homeHealth.note: Prairie geology shows up in cross-Canada radon surveys with above-average shares of homes over the guideline. A $30–$60 long-term winter kit is the answer, new builds included.

homeHealth.name: Deep-cold CO discipline
homeHealth.note: Long furnace seasons and attached garages: alarms adjacent to sleeping areas, checked for expiry, plus annual servicing — and the spillage check before any air-sealing.

homeHealth.name: Smoke-season air
homeHealth.note: Fire smoke reaches Alberta summers most years now. Monitor PM2.5 indoors and size HEPA units to bedrooms.

homeHealth.name: Rural wells
homeHealth.note: Alberta well owners can access provincial lab bacteriological testing through health services — ask your local public health office for the current route, and add periodic chemistry panels.

provinces.name: Saskatchewan
provinces.intro: Saskatchewan's Home Efficiency Retrofit Rebate ended in April 2026, and no rebate has replaced it. What's left is the Home Renovation Tax Credit (10.5%, up to $420 a year), SaskEnergy rebates on high-efficiency gas equipment, and free upgrades for income-qualified homes. Air sealing and insulation still pay back, just through your bills instead of a rebate cheque.
provinces.housing: Wartime and post-war stock in Regina and Saskatoon with empty walls and thin attics, farmhouses exposed to open-prairie wind, and winters that hold deep cold for months. Blower-door numbers here translate to real dollars faster than almost anywhere.

programs.name: Home Efficiency Retrofit Rebate
programs.headline: Ended April 2026
programs.note: SaskPower and SaskEnergy say it ended in April 2026, and SaskEnergy's Energy Efficiency Discounts Program ended July 27, 2026. We list them because much of the internet still advertises them; don't budget around either.

programs.name: Utility offers (SaskEnergy / SaskPower)
programs.headline: Gas equipment rebates · free income-qualified upgrades
programs.note: SaskEnergy pays $325–$1,000 for replacing a gas furnace, boiler or water heater with a high-efficiency model (apply within 120 days). SaskPower's Energy Assistance Program gives income-qualified households free upgrades, including a smart thermostat if eligible, and participants may qualify for SaskEnergy's free furnace upgrade. Neither utility lists a heat pump rebate.

programs.name: Home Renovation Tax Credit
programs.headline: 10.5% · up to $420 a year ($525 seniors)
programs.note: A non-refundable provincial credit for 2025 and later tax years: 10.5% of renovation expenses above $1,000, up to $5,000 ($6,000 for seniors), incurred on or after October 1, 2024 on your principal residence. Windows, doors, furnaces and ventilation qualify; your own labour and appliances don't.

homeHealth.name: Radon — the Prairies' quiet issue
homeHealth.note: Saskatchewan consistently ranks among the higher radon regions in national surveying. Every basement bedroom is a reason to run the winter kit.

homeHealth.name: Farm and rural wells
homeHealth.note: Bacteria plus nitrates near cropland — test on the seasonal rhythm and add chemistry panels; your provincial lab or health office lists the route.

homeHealth.name: Deep-cold humidity swings
homeHealth.note: Winter air this cold drives indoor humidity to extremes — a hygrometer per level tells you whether you're too dry (January) or too damp (July basement).

homeHealth.name: Wood and dual heat CO
homeHealth.note: Dual-fuel and wood-assisted heating is common — in-date alarms by every sleeping area and annual servicing are the baseline.

provinces.name: Manitoba
provinces.intro: Manitoba is one of Canada's better-run efficiency markets: Efficiency Manitoba pays a $400 rebate on the EnerGuide evaluation itself, publishes rebates for windows, heat pumps and insulation, and runs free income-qualified streams.
provinces.housing: Winnipeg's early-1900s cores and post-war rings mirror the classic prairie pattern: solid old bones, empty walls, thin attics, and a winter that finds every leak. Cheap clean hydro power makes electrification math friendlier here than most provinces.

programs.name: Efficiency Manitoba — EnerGuide Evaluation Rebate
programs.headline: $400 back on the evaluation
programs.note: Complete a pre-retrofit EnerGuide evaluation through an approved service organization, plan at least one upgrade within 12 months, and apply within 90 days with your reports — $400 back. The audit-first model, subsidized.

programs.name: Efficiency Manitoba — windows, heat pumps & insulation
programs.headline: Windows $100 · heat pumps $1,500–$2,000 · insulation by R-value
programs.note: $100 per ENERGY STAR triple-pane window or door ($300 income-qualified), $2,000 for a ducted cold-climate heat pump or $1,500 ductless, a no-upfront-cost ground-source option at $75 a month for 15 years, and insulation at $0.03–$0.15 × R-value added × sq ft. Income-qualified households can get a heat pump free, and Manitoba delivers the federal Greener Homes Affordability Program.

homeHealth.name: Radon — top of the national charts
homeHealth.note: Manitoba regularly posts among the highest shares of homes above the radon guideline in cross-Canada surveys. If you do one thing from this page, start the winter kit.

homeHealth.name: Deep-winter CO
homeHealth.note: Months of continuous furnace time: check alarm expiry dates each fall and keep the spillage check in any air-sealing plan.

homeHealth.name: Rural and cottage wells
homeHealth.note: Test on the seasonal rhythm — bacteria often, chemistry periodically — through the provincial route your health office lists.

homeHealth.name: Spring-melt moisture
homeHealth.note: Red River spring moisture finds basements. Hygrometer first, cause before cleanup, and never insulate over a damp assembly.

provinces.name: Ontario
provinces.intro: Ontario is our home turf and the deepest part of this site: the Home Renovation Savings Program's audit-linked rebates, Toronto's HELP loans, CMHC's premium refunds — plus city-by-city guides for twelve markets and a provider directory with verified credentials.
provinces.housing: From pre-Confederation stone to last year's tract builds, Ontario has every housing era in volume. The pattern that matters: pre-1980 stock dominates the resale market, and it's exactly the stock where audits find five-figure savings opportunities.

programs.name: Home Renovation Savings Program
programs.headline: $600 assessment rebate · insulation to $7,700 · heat pumps to $7,500 ($12,000 ground-source)
programs.note: The audit-linked path: pre- and post-retrofit EnerGuide assessments through one of seven approved service organizations unlock the stack, and the follow-up must be done by December 31, 2026. If your gas comes from Kitchener Utilities or Utilities Kingston rather than Enbridge, check eligibility first. Full details in our program tracker.

programs.name: Toronto HELP + CMHC Eco refunds
programs.headline: Low-interest City loans · 25% premium refund
programs.note: Toronto's Home Energy Loan Program funds projects at posted rates (assessment required for most), and CMHC-insured buyers can claim Eco premium refunds. Both verified in the tracker.

homeHealth.name: City-by-city detail
homeHealth.note: Ontario gets the full treatment: twelve city guides with local housing eras, program angles, and monitor-and-test sections from Ottawa's radon belt to London's humidity.

homeHealth.name: Radon
homeHealth.note: Varies house to house across every Ontario geology — the winter kit is the answer everywhere, and Ottawa-area homes especially shouldn't skip it.

homeHealth.name: Free well-water testing
homeHealth.note: Ontario's standout: Public Health Ontario tests private well samples for bacteria free of charge. Rural homeowners — use it seasonally.

homeHealth.name: CO alarms are law
homeHealth.note: The Hawkins-Gignac Act requires alarms near sleeping areas in homes with fuel appliances, fireplaces, or attached garages — Ontario is the province where this is settled law, not just best practice.

provinces.name: Quebec
provinces.intro: Quebec runs two main programs. The government's Rénoclimat pays for insulation and high-performance windows and, since October 1, 2026, no longer requires an evaluation (it pays up to $500 toward one); it also added a flood-protection component. Hydro-Québec's LogisVert pays for heat pumps, roof insulation in electrically heated houses, appliances and solar.
provinces.housing: Montreal's plexes — with their exterior stairs, shared walls, and 1900–1950 bones — are their own retrofit discipline; the regions add farmhouses and mid-century bungalows heated with everything from hydro baseboards to oil. Winters are long enough that envelope work pays even at Quebec's low electricity prices.

programs.name: Rénoclimat
programs.headline: Insulation & windows · evaluation optional since Oct 1, 2026
programs.note: New rules since October 1, 2026: insulation paid per square foot (up to $2,000 for the roof, $7,000 for walls and $2,500 for foundations in a house), ENERGY STAR Most Efficient windows at $300 each, up to $500 toward an optional evaluation, and a new flood-protection Adaptation component. Work must be done by RBQ-licensed contractors, and claims go through a new online portal expected this fall. The old evaluation-first rules apply only if you requested a pre-work evaluation by October 12, 2026.

programs.name: Hydro-Québec LogisVert
programs.headline: Heat pumps $50–$120 per 1,000 BTU/h · roof insulation $1,500
programs.note: Heat pump grants scaled to capacity (ENERGY STAR models required since November 26, 2025; up to $6,700), plus roof insulation with caulking ($1,500 in electrically heated houses), appliances and solar ($1,000/kW). The measure that ended in August 2025 was heat pumps installed with caulking, not roof insulation.

programs.name: Greener Homes Affordability (QC delivery)
programs.headline: 2026–27 registration ended
programs.note: Hydro-Québec's free upgrades for modest-income households, Quebec's delivery of the federal Affordability Program, closed registration for the 2026–27 season and is processing the applications already received.

homeHealth.name: Radon
homeHealth.note: The Appalachian belt and pockets across the province test high; Montreal Island varies block to block. Every home: one winter kit, especially with a basement bedroom or office.

homeHealth.name: Wells in the regions
homeHealth.note: Quebec well owners test through accredited private labs — bacteria seasonally, chemistry periodically. Keep the reports; notaries ask.

homeHealth.name: Plex ventilation
homeHealth.note: Stacked flats with one leaky envelope and no mechanical ventilation are Quebec's signature moisture case — measure the fans, then fix causes.

homeHealth.name: Heating-oil legacies
homeHealth.note: Oil furnaces and their tanks linger in the regions: annual servicing, in-date CO alarms, and — at replacement — LogisVert makes the heat pump the obvious quote to get.

provinces.name: New Brunswick
provinces.intro: New Brunswick's Total Home Energy Savings Program is the classic audit-first design: a home energy evaluation opens the door, and incentives follow the upgrades it recommends — doors, insulation, heating, windows. In a province with real winters and a lot of older wood-frame stock, the sequence works.
provinces.housing: Wood-frame farmhouses and village homes, many predating insulation standards entirely, alongside post-war stock in Moncton, Saint John, and Fredericton. Oil heat's long tail is still being converted out — heat pump adoption here has been among Canada's fastest.

programs.name: Total Home Energy Savings Program
programs.headline: Evaluation $99 + HST · heat pumps $400–$2,000
programs.note: Register with NB Power's SaveEnergyNB, get the Home Energy Evaluation ($99 + HST covers both visits), then complete recommended upgrades within 9 months: attic insulation at $0.40–$0.85 per sq ft, air sealing $250–$550, a central ducted heat pump $1,500, windows and doors $50 each. Oil-to-heat-pump advance payments closed to new registrations June 30, 2026.

programs.name: Enhanced Energy Savings (income-qualified)
programs.headline: Free upgrades, household income under $70,000
programs.note: Homeowners with combined household income under $70,000 may get free upgrades, especially insulation and air sealing.

homeHealth.name: Radon — Atlantic hotspot
homeHealth.note: New Brunswick posts some of Atlantic Canada's highest radon numbers in national surveying. The winter kit belongs on every homeowner's list here.

homeHealth.name: Wells everywhere
homeHealth.note: A huge share of NB homes run on private wells — test bacteria seasonally and chemistry (including arsenic and uranium, real concerns in NB geology) every few years through the provincial route.

homeHealth.name: Oil-heat CO and tanks
homeHealth.note: Remaining oil systems need annual servicing, in-date CO alarms, and honest tank inspections — insurers increasingly force the issue.

homeHealth.name: Wind-driven rain
homeHealth.note: Coastal storms push water into walls that prairie homes never see — moisture diagnosis before insulation is the rule for older envelopes.

provinces.name: Nova Scotia
provinces.intro: Efficiency Nova Scotia (EfficiencyOne) runs one of Canada's most complete program sets: assessment-based rebates for everyone, a moderate-income tier, and HomeWarming's free upgrades for income-qualified households. The federal oil-to-heat-pump money is spent out here and the new federal heat pump rebate won't open until early 2027, so for now the provincial stack is what remains, and it's substantial.
provinces.housing: Canada's oldest housing stock by share in many communities: wood-frame homes that have seen two centuries of Atlantic weather, plus post-war Halifax suburbs. Oil heat's share was long the country's highest — which is why conversion programs hit Nova Scotia first and hardest.

programs.name: Home Energy Assessment path
programs.headline: Assessment $199 · rebates up to $5,000
programs.note: The assessment costs $199 (waived for households under Efficiency Nova Scotia's income threshold) and opens rebates of up to $5,000, including $300–$600 per ton for heat pumps. Finish the work within 12 months of the first assessment.

programs.name: Moderate Income Rebates + HomeWarming
programs.headline: Moderate Income Rebate up to $5,000 more · HomeWarming free
programs.note: The Moderate Income Rebate adds up to $5,000 on top of the standard $5,000 (up to $10,000 in all) for homes not heated mainly by electricity; Efficiency Nova Scotia cut its maximum from $10,000 after the federal oil-to-heat-pump funding ended. HomeWarming installs free upgrades for income-qualified homeowners; renters aren't eligible. NS also delivers the federal Affordability Program through HomeWarming and the African Nova Scotian Communities Retrofit program.

programs.name: Oil to Heat Pump Affordability (NS)
programs.headline: Closed to new applicants July 2, 2026
programs.note: Efficiency Nova Scotia allocated its federal oil-to-heat-pump funding and stopped taking applications on July 2, 2026; the national program closed July 31. If a contractor is still selling it, walk.

homeHealth.name: Radon
homeHealth.note: Nova Scotia's granite and slate geologies produce real radon variation — community results have run high in parts of the mainland. Test over winter, whatever your neighbour's number was.

homeHealth.name: Wells and coastal water
homeHealth.note: Bacteria seasonally, chemistry periodically — with arsenic and uranium on the panel; both show up in NS bedrock wells often enough to test for by default.

homeHealth.name: Wind-driven moisture
homeHealth.note: Two-century-old envelopes plus Atlantic storms: diagnose moisture paths before any insulation project, and treat musty basements as a cause hunt, not a cleaning job.

homeHealth.name: Oil-heat CO
homeHealth.note: The remaining oil fleet needs annual servicing and in-date alarms — and every conversion quote should start from a real heat-loss calculation.

provinces.name: Prince Edward Island
provinces.intro: efficiencyPEI keeps the audit-first path cheap: a $99 + HST subsidized home energy assessment through five approved providers unlocks insulation, window, door and air-sealing rebates. Heat pump rebates ended on April 15, 2026; the new federal heat pump rebate is expected to open in early 2027.
provinces.housing: Island farmhouses and village homes with long exposure to wind and salt air, a post-war ring around Charlottetown, and one of Canada's fastest heat-pump adoption curves — driven by years of aggressive conversion programs.

programs.name: Home Energy Assessment ($99 + HST)
programs.headline: Subsidized audit via 5 partners
programs.note: The entry point: a subsidized EnerGuide-based assessment booked directly with efficiencyPEI's partner firms, producing the report that unlocks the rebate streams.

programs.name: Insulation, window & air-sealing rebates
programs.headline: Windows $125 per opening · free insulation under $55,000
programs.note: After the assessment: insulation rebates by R-value added, $125 per ENERGY STAR window, door or skylight (up to $1,000) and $150–$575 for air sealing, with higher rates for household incomes under $35,000. Households under $55,000 can get insulation free, and PEI delivers the federal Affordability Program.

programs.name: Heat pump rebates
programs.headline: Ended April 15, 2026
programs.note: PEI ended heat pump, heat pump water heater, HRV and solar rebates on April 15, 2026, and free heat pump and oil-to-heat-pump applications are closed. Equipment bought between April 15, 2025 and April 15, 2026 can still be claimed within a year of purchase.

homeHealth.name: Wells and nitrates
homeHealth.note: PEI is Canada's most groundwater-dependent province — everyone's water is well water. Nitrates from the Island's agriculture belong on your testing panel as a standing item.

homeHealth.name: Radon
homeHealth.note: Island sediments vary; homes above the guideline turn up here as everywhere. One winter kit settles your house.

homeHealth.name: Wind-driven rain
homeHealth.note: Exposed island weather works older envelopes hard — check moisture paths before insulating, and keep bath fans terminating outside, not in attics.

homeHealth.name: Heat pump reality check
homeHealth.note: With heat pumps near-universal in new installs, sizing discipline matters: the F280 calculation keeps PEI's favourite upgrade actually performing.

provinces.name: Newfoundland & Labrador
provinces.intro: Newfoundland and Labrador's programs grew in 2026: takeCHARGE's Oil to Electric program pays up to $9,000 toward a central heat pump replacing oil ($22,000 if income-qualified), insulation rebates reach $3,000 in electrically heated homes, and a new no-cost program for income-eligible homes covers projects completed after October 5, 2026.
provinces.housing: St. John's rowhouses and wood-frame stock built long before insulation codes, outport homes facing open-Atlantic weather, and Labrador's subarctic conditions. Electric baseboard's big share makes heat pump math simple on the island grid.

programs.name: takeCHARGE (NL Power / NL Hydro)
programs.headline: Insulation to $3,000 · air sealing · HRV
programs.note: Electrically heated homes get 75% of attic and basement insulation costs (up to $1,000 each, plus up to $500 labour each), $200–$750 for blower-door-tested air sealing, and $225 for an HRV.

programs.name: Oil to Electric Incentive Program
programs.headline: Up to $9,000 · $22,000 income-qualified
programs.note: Still accepting applications, with no closure date set: up to $9,000 for a central heat pump replacing oil or propane ($22,000 if income-qualified), less for mini-splits or electric furnaces; retroactive to April 1, 2023. Pre-approval holds the incentive for 365 days.

programs.name: TakeCharge Greener Homes (income-eligible)
programs.headline: No-cost upgrades, projects after Oct 5, 2026
programs.note: For households under its income limits: up to 100% of approved upgrades, including a limited number of no-cost heat pumps, HRVs, insulation and air sealing, with home energy assessments before and after. Only projects completed after October 5, 2026 qualify.

homeHealth.name: Wind-driven everything
homeHealth.note: Horizontal rain and fog work envelopes like nowhere else in Canada. Moisture diagnosis precedes every insulation decision in older stock.

homeHealth.name: Radon
homeHealth.note: Variable geology, including higher-testing zones — the winter kit answers your house, and finished basements raise the stakes.

homeHealth.name: Outport wells
homeHealth.note: Test bacteria seasonally and chemistry periodically through the provincial route; keep the paper — it matters at resale.

homeHealth.name: Oil and wood CO
homeHealth.note: Oil furnaces and wood stoves both demand annual servicing and in-date alarms adjacent to every sleeping area.

provinces.name: The North (YT · NT · NU)
provinces.intro: The territories run their own programs through organizations built for northern conditions: Yukon's Energy Branch pays the largest heat pump and insulation rebates in the North, the NWT's Arctic Energy Alliance subsidizes EnerGuide evaluations and insulation, and Nunavut's support runs through the Nunavut Housing Corporation.
provinces.housing: Homes engineered for −40 and building on permafrost — where envelope quality isn't a savings project, it's the difference between livable and not. Fuel costs several times southern prices make every measured improvement count double.

programs.name: Yukon — Energy Branch rebates
programs.headline: Heat pumps to $10,500 ($24,000 income-qualified)
programs.note: 50% of heat pump costs up to $10,500 in an existing home, or 100% up to $24,000 through the income-qualified Affordable Heat Pump Program, plus attic insulation ($2,500), above-ground walls (up to $12,000), air sealing ($5,000) and ENERGY STAR windows ($120 each).

programs.name: NWT — Arctic Energy Alliance
programs.headline: Evaluations $200 + GST · insulation rebates
programs.note: The Arctic Energy Alliance subsidizes EnerGuide evaluations ($200 + GST for a house) and pays for insulation (exterior walls up to $8,000), programmable thermostats and wood or pellet stoves. It lists no heat pump rebate and no longer funds fossil-fuel heating.

programs.name: Nunavut — Housing Corporation programs
programs.headline: Homeowner support via the NHC
programs.note: The Nunavut Housing Corporation's homeownership programs offer advice on repairs, renovations, financing and energy conservation. Homes in Nunavut were never eligible for the federal oil-to-heat-pump program because of grid requirements.

homeHealth.name: Radon — Yukon especially
homeHealth.note: Yukon communities have posted some of Canada's highest radon shares in national surveys. Northern basements and crawlspaces deserve the kit as a default.

homeHealth.name: Extreme-cold ventilation
homeHealth.note: At −40, envelope tightness is survival — which makes measured mechanical ventilation non-negotiable. HRVs are standard equipment here for a reason.

homeHealth.name: Fuel systems and CO
homeHealth.note: Oil and propane dominate; alarms, annual servicing, and spillage checks matter more with every degree below zero.

homeHealth.name: Trucked and well water
homeHealth.note: Water systems vary from municipal trucked service to private wells — your territorial health authority sets the testing route; the discipline is the same.
